## Mechanism of Action and Receptor Selectivity
Beta-blockers work by competitively blocking beta-adrenergic receptors. They differ in which receptors they block: beta-1 selective drugs (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) mainly lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective drugs (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block beta-2, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Mixed alpha/beta blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add alpha-1 blockade, leading to vasodilation.
Typical adult doses are once-daily unless noted. For example, metoprolol tartrate is 50-100 mg twice daily, ER 25-200 mg; atenolol 25-100 mg; bisoprolol 1.25-10 mg; carvedilol 3.125-25 mg twice daily; nebivolol 2.5-20 mg; propranolol 40-160 mg three or four times daily (IR) or 80-160 mg LA; sotalol 80-160 mg twice daily.
Indications include hypertension, chronic stable angina, post-MI mortality reduction, HFrEF (with bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol-ER, nebivolol), rate control in AF/flutter, ventricular arrhythmia prophylaxis (sotalol), migraine prophylaxis (propranolol), essential tremor, and glaucoma (topical timolol).

## Pharmacokinetics and Dosing
Beta-blockers work by competitively blocking β-adrenergic receptors. β1-selective agents (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol, nebivolol) lower heart rate, contractility, and renin release. Non-selective agents (propranolol, timolol, nadolol, sotalol) also block β2 receptors, causing bronchoconstriction and reduced peripheral vasodilation. Carvedilol and labetalol add α1-blockade, producing vasodilation.
Pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability is 50% for metoprolol and atenolol, 30% for propranolol (high first-pass). ## Contraindications and Cautions
Beta-blockers are not safe for everyone. They are contraindicated or used with caution in several conditions. In asthma or COPD with reversible bronchospasm, avoid non-selective beta-blockers because they can trigger bronchospasm. In sinus bradycardia (heart rate <50 bpm), 2nd/3rd degree AV block, or sick sinus syndrome, they can worsen bradycardia or heart block. They are also contraindicated in cardiogenic shock and decompensated heart failure, though they can be started once the patient is euvolemic.
In severe peripheral arterial disease, beta-blockers risk ischemia. In pregnancy, atenolol is avoided due to intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR); labetalol is preferred. In diabetes, beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia symptoms, so prefer beta-1 selective agents or nebivolol. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have increased levels of metoprolol and carvedilol, so dose adjustments may be needed.

Abrupt cessation can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia, so taper over 1-2 weeks. ## Drug Interactions
Beta-blockers can worsen asthma or COPD with reversible bronchospasm, especially non-selective ones, so avoid them in such patients. They are also contraindicated in sinus bradycardia below 50 bpm, second or third degree AV block, sick sinus syndrome, cardiogenic shock, and decompensated heart failure unless the patient is euvolemic. Severe peripheral arterial disease is a caution due to risk of ischemia.
In pregnancy, atenolol is avoided because it can cause intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR); labetalol is preferred. Beta-blockers can mask hypoglycemia in diabetic patients, so prefer beta-1 selective agents or nebivolol. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers have increased levels of metoprolol and carvedilol.
Key drug interactions: combining with digoxin, verapamil, diltiazem, or ivabradine increases bradycardia risk. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and diuretics increase hypotension. NSAIDs reduce the antihypertensive effect. CYP2D6 inhibitors like fluoxetine and paroxetine raise metoprolol levels.
Monitoring includes heart rate, blood pressure, ECG for PR/QRS intervals, renal function, electrolytes (especially potassium), glucose, and lipid profile because non-selective beta-blockers can raise triglycerides and lower HDL. Adverse effects range from fatigue, cold extremities, and sexual dysfunction to bronchospasm, masking of hyperglycemia, depression, and heart block.
Abrupt cessation can cause rebound tachycardia, hypertension, and ischemia, so taper over 1–2 weeks. In elderly patients, start low and go slow. In chronic kidney disease, use renally cleared agents like atenolol or nadolol with dose reduction. In heart failure, uptitrate to target doses: bisoprolol 10 mg, carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, or metoprolol-ER 200 mg.
